body.text: With more than 80 per cent of ballots counted in Sweden’s general election held on September 13, the Scandinavian country’s opposition centre-left bloc is clinging to a razor-thin lead, projected to take 176 seats in the 349-member Riksdag against 173 for the incumbent centre-right alliance. Under the country’s proportional representation system, which requires parties to clear a 4 per cent national threshold for seats, little further shift is expected in the final tally.

The Social Democrats, the grand old party of Swedish politics and the largest force in the opposition camp, saw its vote share fall 2.2 percentage points from the previous election—30.3 per cent to 28.1 per cent. Yet it remains on course to lead the next government, thanks to gains by its smaller partners: the Left Party (up 1.5 percentage points), the Greens (up about 1 point), and the Centre Party (up 0.3 to 0.5 points).

On the governing side, the Sweden Democrats, the largest party in the right-wing bloc after the 2022 election, have now fallen behind the Moderates. Goodwill for the two largest parties in the last election has diminished substantially, and people seem to have shown enhanced trust and support for the smaller parties.

Remarkably, neither bloc has crossed the 50 per cent mark. The opposition is hovering around 49.5 per cent and the ruling alliance around 49.0 to 49.1 per cent—a margin of just 0.4 to 0.5 points, equivalent to roughly 28,000–29,000 votes. More than 84,000 ballots were declared invalid, while parties that failed to clear the 4 per cent threshold collected about 1.6 per cent of the vote, or more than 99,000 ballots. Those “wasted” votes could have proved decisive in such a tight contest.

The outcome highlights a paradox often cited in first-past-the-post systems: even pure proportional representation does not guarantee that the winning side will command a majority of the popular vote. Sweden’s result, therefore, reignites debate over whether the 4 per cent threshold should be lowered to improve inclusiveness. A threshold set at one seat’s worth of the national vote—roughly 0.3 per cent (1/349)—would have allowed the smaller parties’ combined 1.6 per cent vote share to translate into five or six seats. In a race this close, those seats could have determined the next government and given a voice to groups that currently go unrepresented.

This logic resonates far beyond Sweden. In the Indian context, under a proportional system, a nomadic or homeless community securing just 0.2 per cent of the national vote would clear the equivalent of one seat in a 543-member Lok Sabha. A party exclusively focused on the rights of the disabled, drawing on a population share of 2.21 per cent according to the 2011 census, might convert a 1 per cent national vote to five seats. Other subaltern groups could likewise gain direct representation rather than seeing their support being dissipated.

As Sweden awaits the final count, the cliffhanger result has already demonstrated that proportional systems, for all their advantages, are not immune to the democratic dilemmas of narrow majorities or manufactured majorities, and to the excluded voices of the subaltern.

The only difference seems to be that in the first-past-the-post system these votes are almost entirely wasted, constituency-wise, while in the proportional representation system, the votes are wasted nationally. Sweden’s cliffhanger results show that proportional representation too can silence minority voices when the threshold is set too high. Lowering it to the mathematical equivalent of one seat would turn such “wasted” ballots into representation—precisely the inclusiveness that the most marginalised communities still lack.
Vipul Anekant is Deputy Commissioner with Delhi Police. Sanjay Kumar is a professor at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS). The views expressed here are personal.
